blocks.text: Paul addresses a dispute between fellow believers that has become public litigation, calling the lawsuits themselves a communal failure while also accusing some members of wrongdoing and fraud. The passage concerns an unidentified insider civil dispute; it should not automatically be applied to crimes, abuse, safety threats, mandatory reporting, or access to impartial courts. Any mediation appropriate to this passage must remain voluntary, impartial, accessible, and attentive to unequal power.

The vice list in verses 9–10 includes two ancient Greek labels whose precise scope is disputed: malakoi has a broad range of “softness” and moral uses, while arsenokoitai is rare. They cannot simply be treated as modern sexual-orientation identities. The warning is followed immediately by “such were some of you” and by language of washing, sanctification, and justification, so the passage does not create permanent categories of contamination or selective stigma.

sections.title: A warning and a changed community

blocks.text: “All things are lawful for me” is likely a saying Paul quotes and qualifies rather than an unrestricted maxim. His reply tests freedom by benefit and by mastery: a person must not be brought under a thing’s power. In the wider argument, freedom is therefore not a reason to override another person’s safety, consent, or material welfare.

Verses 12–20 link resurrection, belonging to Messiah, bodily union, the Spirit’s temple, being “bought with a price,” and glorifying God in the body. The argument treats embodied life as significant rather than disposable. Its imagined example is a male assembly member joining a prostitute, yet it gives no account of the woman’s legal, economic, or coercive circumstances; that silence cautions against stigma and requires attention to unequal power, slavery, and exploitation.

Calling the body a temple of the Holy Spirit affirms embodied dignity; it cannot support body shame, purity surveillance, disability stigma, or medical neglect. Likewise, the language of being “bought with a price,” drawn from a slaveholding world, does not make a spouse, church leader, or any other person the owner of someone else’s body.
